Ōsugi Shrine (Ōsugi Jinja) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Aba, Inashiki City, [[Ibaraki Prefecture]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Osugi Shrine {{!}} Visit {{!}} IBARAKI GUIDE|url=https://visit.ibarakiguide.jp/en/sightseeing/22351/|access-date=2024-03-29|website=visit.ibarakiguide.jp|language=en-US}}</ref> It is known as the "[[Nikkō Tōshō-gū]] of [[Ibaraki Prefecture|Ibaraki]]" due to its lavish shrine buildings and is affectionately called "Anba-sama." The shrine has historically been known by names such as Ōsugi Dai-myōjin, Ōsugi Daigongen, and Imamiya Ōsugi Dai-myōjin. The [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|former shrine ranking]] was a village shrine. It is currently designated as a "[[Beppyo shrine|Beppyo Jinja]]" by the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. It serves as the head shrine for about 670 Ōsugi Shrines distributed across the [[Kantō region|Kantō]] and [[Tōhoku region|Tōhoku regions]].
== Deities Worshiped == [[File:Osugi-shrine_festival,Inashiki-city,Japan.jpg|right|thumb|254x254px| Awa floats at the Osugi Shrine festival]]
;Main deity : [[Yamato Okunitama|Yamato]] [[Ōmononushi|Omononushi Kushimikatama]] no Mikoto ; Enshrined : [[Ōkuninushi|Okuninushi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Sukunabikona|Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto]]
Initially, the shrine enshrined Yamato Ōmono Nushi Kushi Mikatama no Mikoto from Ōmiya Shrine in Yamato Province. In 1241, [[Ōkuninushi|Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] and [[Sukunabikona|Sukunahikona no Mikoto]] were also enshrined from {{ill|10=ja|11=今宮神社_(京都市)|Imamiya Shrine|en}}. The configuration of deities mirrors that of [[Ōmiwa Shrine|Ōmiya Shrine]]. The shrine's name derives from a large [[Cryptomeria japonica]] tree within its grounds, originally part of a trio of cedars named Tarōsugi, Jirōsugi, and Saburōsugi, though Tarōsugi was destroyed by fire in 1778.
The shrine is also associated with the tengu, mythical creatures in Japanese folklore, specifically the "Hana-taka Tengu" and "Karasu Tengu." During the Bunji era (1185-1189), a retainer of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitsune|en}} named {{ill|10=ja|11=常陸坊海尊|Hitachibō Kaison}} performed various miracles attributed to the divine virtue of the great cedar. This led to the belief that prayers made through Kaison would be fulfilled by the great cedar deity. Kaison, resembling a tengu, helped establish the tengu belief through his image, leading to the recognition of Hana-taka Tengu and Karasu Tengu as guardian deities. Hana-taka Tengu is known as the "Wish-fulfilling Tengu," and Karasu Tengu as the "Granting Tengu," believed to bestow blessings and fulfill wishes.
It worships a rarely worshipped [[kami]] named Anba sama.<ref name=":0" />
== History == According to the shrine's website, the area of "Anba" belonged to the ancient national creation system before the Ritsuryō system, being part of the Uda Province. Ōsugi Shrine was the most important shrine venerating the Uda no Kuni no miyatsuko.
In ancient times, the Awa region, part of the plateau where the shrine is located, protruded into the seas called "Shinoda Ryūkai" (west coast of Lake Kasumigaura) and "Enoura Ryūkai" (part of the Tone River's lowland area). Awa was positioned deeply within an inland bay surrounded by Awasaki and Sugatsu, and a large cedar there was worshipped by fishermen and served as a navigational landmark for ships sailing the internal sea (Katori Inner Sea or Jōsō Inner Sea).
=== "Nohama" and "Anpa no Shima" === The Hitachi Province Fudoki records names such as "Nohama" and "Anpa no Shima" as part of Awa. "Nohama" appeared in the entries for Shinoda District, and "Anpa no Shima" appeared in the entries for Namegata District, with additional historical significance and mythological accounts associated with these areas.
=== Construction === The shrine was reportedly established in 767. Over centuries, it has faced various disasters and reconstructions, continuing to serve as a central place of worship and community gathering, intertwined deeply with local history and legend.
=== Middle Ages to Modern Period === During the Genryaku and Bunji eras (1184-1190), a legend says that Hitachibō Kaison, believed to be an incarnation or a divine messenger of the great cedar deity, aided Minamoto no Yoshitsune in his campaigns against the Taira clan. After these events, he mysteriously disappeared in 1189, leaving a lasting impression that he was a divine servant of the great deity.
In 1241, the Imamiya Shrine in Kyoto's sacred spirits of Ōkuninushi no Mikoto and Sukunahikona no Mikoto were transferred to Ōsugi Shrine, renaming it Imamiya Ōsugi Daigongen.
During the Onin War (1467-1477), the shrine's territories were plundered, but in the Keichō era (1596-1615), the Tokugawa shogunate granted the shrine land and exempted it from duties. The control of shrine affairs was transferred to Tendai Sect's Enryaku-ji Temple under the command of the monk Tenkai.
Tenkai himself played a significant role by integrating the shrine into the protective system for Edo Castle, emphasizing its importance in warding off evil from the northeastern direction, traditionally considered unlucky in Japanese geomancy.
=== Edo Period Developments === The association with Tenkai and subsequent events further elevated the shrine’s status. During severe droughts, Tenkai performed rainmaking rituals invoking the shrine's deities, purportedly leading to miraculous rainfalls that affirmed the shrine’s spiritual potency.
=== Modern Era === After the Meiji Restoration in 1868, which mandated the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, the shrine's Buddhist affiliations were dissolved, reaffirming its purely Shinto identity.
In 1871, during the first prefectural integrations, the shrine was included in the newly formed Niiji Prefecture, later becoming part of Ibaraki Prefecture in 1875. It was classified as a village shrine in 1881 and later elevated to the status of a county shrine.
The shrine saw multiple reconstructions due to fires in the 18th and 19th centuries, notably in 1798 and again in 1802. Each time, the community and its patrons rallied to restore and maintain the shrine structures, culminating in substantial rebuilding efforts in the early 19th century supported by imperial donations and local efforts.
=== Cultural Impact === Ōsugi Shrine has played a significant role in regional cultural practices, including the "Anba-sama" folklore, which spread across the Pacific coast of the Kantō and Tōhoku regions. This includes rituals for warding off smallpox and ensuring safe water transport, highlighting the shrine’s central role in the everyday lives and spiritual practices of the local communities.
=== Recognition and Preservation === In modern times, the shrine continues to be an important cultural and religious site, with ongoing restoration projects and celebrations that attract visitors and worshippers from across Japan and beyond. It was designated as an important cultural property and continues to participate actively in preserving and sharing local traditions and history.
*
== History == According to the "History of Osugi Shrine" on the shrine's website, the land of "Anba" belonged to Ukami Province (Umi Province) under the kuni no miyatsuko [[Kuni no miyatsuko|system]] that existed before {{ill|10=ja|11=律令制|the Ritsuryo system}}, and "Osugi Shrine was the most important shrine dedicated to [[:ja:下海上国造|the Ukami kuni no miyatsuko]] ."
In ancient times, the plateau to which Awa belonged was a peninsula jutting out into the Shinda Current Sea (the western part of [[Lake Kasumigaura]] ) and the Enoura Current Sea (an inland sea that spread out in the lowlands of the Tone River basin), and there was {{ill|10=ja|11=浮島村_(茨城県)|a floating island}} off to the northeast. Awa was located at the back of an inland bay (Amatari of Lake Kasumigaura) surrounded by Awazaki and Sugatsu. [[:ja:スギ|The giant cedar tree]] in this area is believed to be the guardian deity of fishermen and also serves as [[:ja:航路標識|a navigational marker]] for the inland seas (Katori Inland Sea or Joso Inland Sea).
=== "Norihama" and "Abanoshi Island" === In the [[:ja:常陸国風土記|Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki]], place names that are thought to refer to the Awa region include "Norihama" in the section on Shinoda County and "Aba no Shima" in the section on Namegata County.
" '''Norihama''' " 「'''乗濱'''」appears in the description of "Norimano Village" in the section on [[:ja:信太郡|Shinoda County]] . When [[:ja:ヤマトタケル|Emperor Yamato Takeru]] was touring the coast and came to Norihama, he saw that there were many people drying seaweed in Hamaura, so the village came to be called "Norimahama." Also, to the east of Norihama-sato is Ukishima-mura, which is surrounded by sea on all sides, and the farmers there made their living by producing salt.
" '''Aba no Shima''' " 「'''安婆之島'''」appears in the description of Takekazama no Mikoto's view of the country in the section on [[:ja:行方郡_(茨城県)|Namegata County]] . Takekarima no Mikoto was camping on "Abanoshi Island" and saw smoke in a bay far in the eastern sea. He made a vow that if it was the smoke of a heavenly being, he would cover him, but if it was the smoke of bandits, he would let it drift into the sea. When the smoke shot out to sea and drifted away, he realized that a vicious bandit (Kunisu) was there. After Takeshikamado murdered Kunisu, the place where it was said he would kill him painfully became "Itakunogo," the place where it was said he would kill him normally became "Butsunanomura," the place where it was said he would kill him cheaply became "Abakinosato," and the place where it was said he would kill him well became "Yoshimaenomura." According to the "Hyōchū Kofudoki," "Itaku" is "Itako," "Futsuna" is "Furutaka," "Abari" is "Awadai" in Furutaka, and "Yoshizaki" is "Ezaki" in [[:ja:延方村|Nobukata village]], all of which became place names in [[:ja:潮来市|Itako City]], located across from "Aba Island."
Awa belonged to "Takada-go" (Shinpen Hitachi Kokushi) or "Norihama-go" ( [[:ja:大日本地名辞書|Dai Nippon Chimei Jisho]] ) mentioned in the " [[:ja:和名類聚抄|Wamyo Ruijusho]] ". The New Hitachi Kokushikan states, "In ancient times, the southwestern part of this town was entirely covered with reeds and a land of deep mud, while the northeastern part was, as it is today, a flowing sea, so it was really like a single island. What was once called Abana Island was probably the area of the two towns of Takada and Norihama (this can be known from the current names of Yasuba Village, Awazaki Village, etc.)." It states that the two towns of Takada and Norihama were the "Aba no Shima" and "Norihama" mentioned in the Hitachi Koku Fudoki. Even today, the area from Isazu to Sugazu in Inashiki City is a peninsula-like or island-like plateau. Regarding the description of Namegata County, it says, "It is said that one crossed the inland sea from Ababa Island to Itarai. The present-day Awazaki and Itarai are opposite each other and are in the same direction, so there is no doubt that what is referred to as Ababa Island here is the area of Takada and Norihama," and the place where Takekashima no Mikoto looked into the country is stated to be "Awazaki." The Great Japanese Place Name Dictionary states, "The Ababa Island mentioned in the Kofudoki probably corresponds to the corresponding Ukishima Island or Awazaki," and the Annotated Kofudoki states, "This so-called Ababa Island is probably the location of Ukishima Island. Now, on Ukishima Island, there is Aba Myojin Shrine, where the deity worshipped is Okuninushi no Mikoto. Aba Village is also worshipped, and the local name is Osugi Myojin." These are some of the views that it is a "floating island."
Incidentally, the note in the "Hyōchū Kofudoki" states that there is an "Yaba Myojin Shrine" on Ukishima, and an "Osugi Myojin Shrine" in Yaba village which enshrines the same deity. Regarding "Yasuba Myojin Shrine," the note in the separate description of "Ukishima no Chomiya" also states, "Ukishima, in the middle of Lake Shintai, is now Ariyasuba Myojin Shrine, this is it." The "Yasuba Myojin Shrine" which the "Hyōchū Kofudoki" identifies with "Chomiya" is thought to refer to the present-day Ojima Shrine. Ojima Shrine enshrines Onamuchino-mikoto (another name for Okuninushi-no-mikoto) as its main deity, and within the shrine grounds there is a stone monument commemorating the site of the "Chomiya" shrine. The "Osugi Myojin" of Yasuba village is thought to refer to the current Osugi Shrine.
=== Founded === It is said to have been founded in the first year of [[Jingo-keiun|the Jingo Keiun]] era ( 767 ).
The "Osugi Shrine Brief History" states that the monk [[:ja:勝道|Shodo]] visited the area, which was suffering from an epidemic, on his way to [[Nikkō|Nikko]] in [[Shimotsuke Province]] . He used the giant cedar as [[Himorogi|a sacred tree]] to enslave '''[[Ōmiwa Shrine|Miwa Myojin]]''' (Okami Shrine) and performed numerous miracles to save the people, which is why the shrine came to be worshiped as the "Anbasama of Demon Barae" <ref>「あんば」とは、当時入り海であった霞ケ浦に突き出た半島を「安婆島」と呼んでおり、その地に大杉神社が作られたことに由来する</ref> <ref>{{Citation|last=柳正博|title=利根川の水神信仰|date=3月|volume=2|pages=82|year=1989|series=調査研究報告|publisher=埼玉県立さきたま資料館|和書}}</ref> . The history of the Inashiki branch of the Ibaraki Prefecture [[:ja:神社庁|Shrine Association]] states, "Seeing that the villagers were suffering greatly from the epidemic, he took pity on them and performed a ritual to appease the Omiwa-no-Okami of Yamato Province under a large cedar tree, and the villagers immediately made a full recovery." However, regarding the sacred object, there are sources which say that it is not the giant cedar itself, but the "spiritual deity Fudo Myo-o" carved by the monk Shotodo, such as "It is Fudo Myo-o, the spiritual deity who subdues demons, carved by the monk Shotodo during the Jingo Keiun era" (Tonegawa Zushi) and "The sacred object is the spiritual deity Fudo Myo-o, the spiritual deity who subdues demons, carved by the monk Shotodo during the Jingo Keiun era" (Jozan Sosui).
In the 15th year [[Enryaku|of the Enryaku era]] (796) or in May of the same year (Inashiki County Local History), Kaiken Ajari of [[:ja:延暦寺|Enryaku-ji]] Temple prayed at Osugi Shrine for the surrender of [[:ja:悪路王|King Akujo]] (Takamaru). The [[:ja:利根川図志|Tonegawa Zushi]] states, "Dengyo Daishi himself came to this place begging for a statue of [[Maitreya|Acala]], who subdues the four demons, which he had carved himself, and after a spiritual dream he enshrined it here, just like Osugi Daimyojin. He also enshrined the statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva, made by Konsuji Katsukura from [[:ja:天竺|India]], thus founding a sacred temple and naming it Ryukozan An'on-ji." It says that he enshrined the "Acala, who subdues the four demons," made by Dengyo Daishi ( [[:ja:最澄|Saicho]] ), along with the "Osugi Daimyojin (spiritual deity Acala)," and further established Ryukozan [[安穏寺 (結城市)|An'on-ji]] with the "statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva," made by Konsuji Katsukura from India, as the principal image. As a reward for his prayers for peace in the nation, he was granted a sacred land, and according to the Inashiki branch, a shrine to "Osugi Daimyojin" was subsequently constructed within the grounds of An'on-ji Temple.
The shrine's website states that An'on-ji Temple was founded in 805 .
The New Compilation of Hitachi Kokushi states, "There is a shrine to Osugi Myojin within the temple grounds. Although this shrine was built later, people from far and wide revered it so much that over time, a shrine building was constructed, and as a result, this temple has become truly like [[:ja:別当寺|a beneficiary]] ." It states that originally there was An'on-ji Temple, and later Osugi Myojin was enshrined there as a shrine within the temple grounds, but the roles of master and servant were reversed due to the extreme reverence. This corresponds to the description in the Inashiki branch, which says that the temple was granted a sacred land in recognition of its meritorious efforts at praying for peace for the nation, centered around Ryukazan An'on-ji Temple, and that "Osugi Daimyojin" was later constructed within the temple grounds. It is possible that Osugi Daimyojin had been worshiped even before that, without having a shrine building.
=== Middle Ages === The Tonegawa Zushi from [[Genryaku|the Genryaku]] and [[Bunji (era)|Bun'ichi]] eras (1184-1190) states, "Osugi Daimyojin resented the rampage of the Taira [[Taira clan|clan]] and appeared as Hitachibo Kaison, who assisted Judge Minamoto no Yoshitsune in defeating the Taira clan. After his success, he returned to this place and carved a statue of himself, which he presented to Osugi Palace." There is a legend that Hitachibo Kaison was [[Incarnation|an incarnation]] of Osugi Daimyojin or [[Shinshi|a divine messenger]] (attachment). On September 27, 1189, he disappeared suddenly on a rainbow of colorful clouds, and "people came to know that Kaisonbo was an associate of the great deity" (Osugi Myojin Ryaku Engi). In the past, an annual festival was held on September 27th, the day Hitachibo Kaison disappeared.
In 1241, [[Ninji|the]] Jozan Sosui records that "a branch of the spirit of Imamiya Shrine in Murasakino, Kyoto was enshrined and the shrine was renamed Imamiya Osugi Daigongen," and the two '''deities Okuninushi no Mikoto''' and '''Sukunahikona no Mikoto''' were [[:ja:分霊|enshrined]] together from [[:ja:今宮神社_(京都市)|Imamiya Shrine]] in [[:ja:京都|Kyoto]] .
During [[Ōnin War|the Onin War]] (1467-1477), the temple's land was plundered, but during [[Keichō|the Keicho]] era (1596-1615), [[Tokugawa shogunate|the Tokugawa shogunate]] granted An'on-ji Temple a fief of 20 koku (Shinpen Hitachi Kokushi) and [[:ja:朱印状|a red seal]] exempting it from various taxes. Additionally, the Tonegawa Scenic Spot Guide states, "The monk [[:ja:天海|Tenkai]] of Mt. Hiei was ordered to take on the role of betto priest concurrently, and from then on all shrine affairs at Annon- [[:ja:寛永寺|ji were handled by Toei-zan]] ," and the temple came under the control of Toei-zan Kan'ei-ji.
Regarding Tenkai's achievements, the "Brief History of Osugi Shrine" states, "Tenkai floated a boat in Tojo Bay and invited Osugi Daimyojin, who is enshrined to the east of the bay, to visit him. He performed a ritual that made it rain beautifully, and performed a miracle." "He designated this shrine as the guardian shrine of the evil spirits direction of [[Edo Castle]], and became the chief priest of his own betto An'on-ji temple." "Due to Tenkai's connection with this shrine, Betto An'on-ji temple became a direct affiliated temple of [[:ja:輪王寺|Nikkozan Rinnoji temple]] ." The information board within the shrine grounds also says that the Osugi no Okami that Tenkai enshrined when he prayed for rain was a "dragon god."
* Tenkai (Zuifu) was invited by [[:ja:蘆名義広|Ashina Yoshihiro]], who became the lord of Edosaki Castle, and served as the chief priest of Edosaki Fudoin Temple from [[Tenshō (Momoyama period)|1570]] to 1603. During this time, there is an anecdote that in [[Bunroku|1594]], in response to a plea from the people of [[Hitachi Province]], who were suffering from a drought, he prayed for [[Rain dance|rain]] . When Tenkai was about to pray for rain at Takada Bay, a girl appeared from the shade of a willow tree and handed him [[:ja:金剛杵|a five-pronged vajra]] (five-pronged vajra) to use in the prayer, then left. As she prayed for rain, lightning flashed from the five-pronged vajra and the image of [[:ja:文殊菩薩|Manjusri Bodhisattva]] riding [[Lion|a lion]] appeared for a moment, and he realized that his daughter was an incarnation of Manjusri Bodhisattva. The people who were saved from the drought expressed their gratitude to Manjusri Bodhisattva and praised Tenkai's virtues. This rain-making story is also recorded in the "History of the Founder of Mount Toei, Jigen Daishi" . Osugi Shrine does not appear to appear in these tales. * The New Compilation of Hitachi Kokushi describes Annon-ji Temple as "a Tendai sect temple, a branch of Ono Hozen-ji Temple, and known as Ryuge-san Jison-in Temple," and according to [[:ja:本末制度|the branch temple system]], it was a branch temple of [[:ja:逢善寺|Hozen-ji Temple]] in Ono, Inashiki City.
In 1725 (the 10th year of the [[Kyōhō|Kyoho]] era), the "Demon-Exorcising Music" began, and as it spread, worship of him as a god for warding off [[smallpox]] and for water traffic spread throughout the Kanto region and the [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific]] coast of Tohoku. Its origins date back to [[Genna|1617]], when Genba Tanaka (the founder of [[:ja:ヒゲタ醤油|Higeta Soy Sauce]] ) brought it from [[Kii Province|Kishu]] along with the Twelve Seats Kagura dance. There is an entry for “Anbasama (Awa-sama)” in the Daijisen Digital [[:ja:大辞泉|Dictionary]], which describes it as “a god worshipped in fishing villages along the Pacific coast from Chiba Prefecture to the Tohoku region."
In 1778, the sacred tree, Taro Cedar, was burned down.
In 1798, both the [[Kansei|shrine]] and temple were destroyed by fire.
[[Kyōwa|In]] 1802, a fire broke out again.
In [[Bunka|1813]], following repeated fires, "the difficulty of restoration reached the attention of Imperial Princess Kinen, the 9th abbot of Rinno-ji Temple, who bestowed 1,000 ryo of gold" (Inashiki County Local History), and "the current shrine building was constructed with the 1,000 ryo of gold that [[:ja:一品親王|the first rank prince]] bestowed on it" (Inashiki Branch), and the shrine was rebuilt. Shortly afterwards, in the Bunsei 12th year (1815), the Sojo Nikki recorded that "Osugi Myojin is said to be the name of Hitachibo Kaison, and although the shrine grounds are modern, it is very lively. (There is also an Osugi shrine in Kashima.)" (Dai Nippon Chimei Jisho). The relocation took place in Bunka 13 (1816) .
=== After the Meiji Period === After [[Meiji Restoration|the Meiji Restoration]], due to the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, Annon-ji Temple was abolished and turned into [[Shinto shrine|a shrine office]] .
On [[Meiji period|November]] 14, 1871, Niiharu Prefecture was established as a result of the first merger of prefectures, and the Niiharu Prefectural Central Teaching Institute was established at Osugi Shrine ("A Brief History of Osugi Shrine").
In October 1873, it was ranked as a village shrine. By the way, in the "Photographic Album of Ibaraki Prefecture Shrines" published in [[Shōwa period|1942]], it was a village shrine, but in the Shrine Details Database held by the National Institute of Japanese Literature, it has been promoted to a village shrine.
On May 7, 1875, Ibaraki Prefecture was established as a result of the second merger of prefectures.
In 1878, An'on-ji Temple was rebuilt.
In April 1907, it merged with the unranked Ise Shrine ( [[Amaterasu|Dainichikagamine]] ) in [[:ja:阿波村_(茨城県)|Awa Village]] .
On January 31, 1978, “Anba-bayashi” was designated [[:ja:記録作成等の措置を講ずべき無形の民俗文化財|an intangible folk cultural property for which measures such as recording are required]] .
In 1982, it became a specially designated shrine under the Shinto Shrines Association.
Construction and repair work began in [[Heisei period|1996]] as part of the Heisei Great Construction Project.
Restoration work on the shrine building (Osugiden) was completed in 2006.
== Shrine grounds == The names of the enshrined deities are listed on explanatory boards within the temple grounds.
* A shrine located in the northwest of the temple grounds.
: Deities enshrined at '''Okuni Shrine''' : [[Ōkuninushi|Okuninushi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Kotoshironushi]] -no- : '''Deity of Ise Shrine''' - [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Omikami]] : '''Hakusan Shrine''' Deity [[:ja:菊理媛神|-Kikurihime]] : Deities worshipped at '''the four shrines''' - [[:ja:カミムスビ|Ame-no-]] [[Ame-no-Minakanushi|Minaka-nushi, Takami-]] [[:ja:タカミムスビ|musubi-no-Kami, Kami-musubi-no-Kami,]] [[Amaterasu]] [[:ja:神直日神|-Omikami, Kaminao-no-Kami,]] and [[:ja:直毘神|O-nao-no-Kami]] : '''Tenmangu Shrine''' Deity - [[Sugawara no Michizane]]
* A shrine located in the southeast of the temple grounds.
: '''[[:ja:大杉神社|Inari Shrine]]''' (Shoichii Ryūshin Sōsei Saisho Inari Daimyojin) Deity - Ukemome : '''Deity of Katsuma''' Shrine - Unknown : '''Aioi Shrine'''
* The Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Photo Album lists three shrines as follows: Inari Shrine (Ukemochi no Mikoto), Hakusan Shrine (Kukurihime no Mikoto), and Okuni Shrine (Onamochi no Mikoto, Sukunahikona no Mikoto). * The Inashiki branch of the Ibaraki Prefectural Shrine Association has four shrines: Inari Shrine, Hakusan Shrine, Okuni Shrine, and Isose Shrine.
=== Katsuma Shrine === Katsuma Shrine is located in the southeast of the temple grounds. The enshrined deity is unknown.
Its ancient name was "Magisha" and it has its own ancient history. "Bareki" means the joists of a stable (the cross beams that support the floorboards), and by extension refers to a manger or the stable itself. "Umatakagami" is the guardian deity of horses and is also known as "Umayanokami" ( [[:ja:厩神|stable god]] ), and is a part of folk beliefs in various regions.
[[Heian period|During the Heian period]], Shinda Horse Ranch (mentioned in [[Engishiki|the Engishiki]] ) was located in Shinda [[:ja:美浦村|, Miho Village]], one of the various [[:ja:諸国牧|ranches]] in Hitachi Province (ranches under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Military Affairs), and [[Jōgan|a shrine]] was established there in 862 to protect the horses. When the horse pasture was abolished at the end of the Heian period, it was passed through Koda [[:ja:稲敷市|in Inashiki City]], and then moved to the grounds of Osugi Shrine during the Kamakura period. There used to be a horse racing track behind Annon-ji Temple (Okuyama), where horse races were held until the early [[Shōwa period|Showa]] period. The stone shrine was enshrined in a place overlooking the track. With the disappearance of farm horses, the shrine was forgotten, but in 2002 a shrine building was constructed on the same site and the shrine was moved there .
Currently, people from [[:ja:日本中央競馬会|the Japan]] Racing Association (JRA) [[:ja:美浦トレーニングセンター|Miho Training Center]], which is located on the site of the ancient Shinta Horse Ranch, come to offer [[Prayer|prayers]] for the year, along with those from the headquarters. It is also well known among horse racing fans. Incidentally, [[:ja:神馬|the sacred horse]] currently used in the Osugi Shrine festival is borrowed from the Miho Training Center because the farmer no longer has any horses left. Many horseshoes have been donated in front of the shrine, and there are also rare charms such as "winning horse charms," "horseshoe votive plaques," and "mane charms."

Ōsugi Shrine (Ōsugi Jinja) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Aba, Inashiki City, [[Ibaraki Prefecture]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Osugi Shrine {{!}} Visit {{!}} IBARAKI GUIDE|url=https://visit.ibarakiguide.jp/en/sightseeing/22351/|access-date=2024-03-29|website=visit.ibarakiguide.jp|language=en-US}}</ref> It is known as the "[[Nikkō Tōshō-gū]] of [[Ibaraki Prefecture|Ibaraki]]" due to its lavish shrine buildings and is affectionately called "Anba-sama." The shrine has historically been known by names such as Ōsugi Dai-myōjin, Ōsugi Daigongen, and Imamiya Ōsugi Dai-myōjin. The [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|former shrine ranking]] was a village shrine. It is currently designated as a "[[Beppyo shrine|Beppyo Jinja]]" by the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. It serves as the head shrine for about 670 Ōsugi Shrines distributed across the [[Kantō region|Kantō]] and [[Tōhoku region|Tōhoku regions]].
== Deities Worshiped == [[File:Osugi-shrine_festival,Inashiki-city,Japan.jpg|right|thumb|254x254px| Awa floats at the Osugi Shrine festival]]
;Main deity : [[Yamato Okunitama|Yamato]] [[Ōmononushi|Omononushi Kushimikatama]] no Mikoto ; Enshrined : [[Ōkuninushi|Okuninushi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Sukunabikona|Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto]]
Initially, the shrine enshrined Yamato Ōmono Nushi Kushi Mikatama no Mikoto from Ōmiya Shrine in Yamato Province. In 1241, [[Ōkuninushi|Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] and [[Sukunabikona|Sukunahikona no Mikoto]] were also enshrined from {{ill|10=ja|11=今宮神社_(京都市)|Imamiya Shrine|en}}. The configuration of deities mirrors that of [[Ōmiwa Shrine|Ōmiya Shrine]]. The shrine's name derives from a large [[Cryptomeria japonica]] tree within its grounds, originally part of a trio of cedars named Tarōsugi, Jirōsugi, and Saburōsugi, though Tarōsugi was destroyed by fire in 1778.
The shrine is also associated with the tengu, mythical creatures in Japanese folklore, specifically the "Hana-taka Tengu" and "Karasu Tengu." During the Bunji era (1185-1189), a retainer of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitsune|en}} named {{ill|10=ja|11=常陸坊海尊|Hitachibō Kaison}} performed various miracles attributed to the divine virtue of the great cedar. This led to the belief that prayers made through Kaison would be fulfilled by the great cedar deity. Kaison, resembling a tengu, helped establish the tengu belief through his image, leading to the recognition of Hana-taka Tengu and Karasu Tengu as guardian deities. Hana-taka Tengu is known as the "Wish-fulfilling Tengu," and Karasu Tengu as the "Granting Tengu," believed to bestow blessings and fulfill wishes.
It worships a rarely worshipped [[kami]] named Anba sama.<ref name=":0" />
== History == According to the shrine's website, the area of "Anba" belonged to the ancient [[kuni no miyatsuko]] system before the Ritsuryō system, being part of the Uda Province. Ōsugi Shrine was the most important shrine venerating the [[:ja:下海上国造|Ukami kuni no miyatsuko]].
In ancient times, the Awa region, part of the plateau where the shrine is located, protruded into the seas called "Shinoda Ryūkai" (west coast of [[Lake Kasumigaura]]) and "Enoura Ryūkai" (an inland sea that spread out in the lowlands of the Tone River basin). Awa was positioned deeply within an inland bay surrounded by Awasaki and Sugatsu, and a large cedar there was worshipped by fishermen and served as a navigational landmark for ships sailing the internal sea (Katori Inner Sea or Jōsō Inner Sea).
=== "Norihama" and "Abanoshi Island" === In the [[:ja:常陸国風土記|Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki]], place names that are thought to refer to the Awa region include "Norihama" in the section on Shinoda County and "Aba no Shima" in the section on Namegata County.
" '''Norihama''' " 「'''乗濱'''」appears in the description of "Norimano Village" in the section on [[:ja:信太郡|Shinoda County]] . When [[:ja:ヤマトタケル|Emperor Yamato Takeru]] was touring the coast and came to Norihama, he saw that there were many people drying seaweed in Hamaura, so the village came to be called "Norimahama." Also, to the east of Norihama-sato is Ukishima-mura, which is surrounded by sea on all sides, and the farmers there made their living by producing salt.
" '''Aba no Shima''' " 「'''安婆之島'''」appears in the description of Takekazama no Mikoto's view of the country in the section on [[:ja:行方郡_(茨城県)|Namegata County]] . Takekarima no Mikoto was camping on "Abanoshi Island" and saw smoke in a bay far in the eastern sea. He made a vow that if it was the smoke of a heavenly being, he would cover him, but if it was the smoke of bandits, he would let it drift into the sea. When the smoke shot out to sea and drifted away, he realized that a vicious bandit (Kunisu) was there. After Takeshikamado murdered Kunisu, the place where it was said he would kill him painfully became "Itakunogo," the place where it was said he would kill him normally became "Butsunanomura," the place where it was said he would kill him cheaply became "Abakinosato," and the place where it was said he would kill him well became "Yoshimaenomura." According to the "Hyōchū Kofudoki," "Itaku" is "Itako," "Futsuna" is "Furutaka," "Abari" is "Awadai" in Furutaka, and "Yoshizaki" is "Ezaki" in [[:ja:延方村|Nobukata village]], all of which became place names in [[:ja:潮来市|Itako City]], located across from "Aba Island."
Awa belonged to "Takada-go" (Shinpen Hitachi Kokushi) or "Norihama-go" ( [[:ja:大日本地名辞書|Dai Nippon Chimei Jisho]] ) mentioned in the " [[:ja:和名類聚抄|Wamyo Ruijusho]] ". The New Hitachi Kokushikan states, "In ancient times, the southwestern part of this town was entirely covered with reeds and a land of deep mud, while the northeastern part was, as it is today, a flowing sea, so it was really like a single island. What was once called Abana Island was probably the area of the two towns of Takada and Norihama (this can be known from the current names of Yasuba Village, Awazaki Village, etc.)." It states that the two towns of Takada and Norihama were the "Aba no Shima" and "Norihama" mentioned in the Hitachi Koku Fudoki. Even today, the area from Isazu to Sugazu in Inashiki City is a peninsula-like or island-like plateau. Regarding the description of Namegata County, it says, "It is said that one crossed the inland sea from Ababa Island to Itarai. The present-day Awazaki and Itarai are opposite each other and are in the same direction, so there is no doubt that what is referred to as Ababa Island here is the area of Takada and Norihama," and the place where Takekashima no Mikoto looked into the country is stated to be "Awazaki." The Great Japanese Place Name Dictionary states, "The Ababa Island mentioned in the Kofudoki probably corresponds to the corresponding Ukishima Island or Awazaki," and the Annotated Kofudoki states, "This so-called Ababa Island is probably the location of Ukishima Island. Now, on Ukishima Island, there is Aba Myojin Shrine, where the deity worshipped is Okuninushi no Mikoto. Aba Village is also worshipped, and the local name is Osugi Myojin." These are some of the views that it is a "floating island."
Incidentally, the note in the "Hyōchū Kofudoki" states that there is an "Yaba Myojin Shrine" on Ukishima, and an "Osugi Myojin Shrine" in Yaba village which enshrines the same deity. Regarding "Yasuba Myojin Shrine," the note in the separate description of "Ukishima no Chomiya" also states, "Ukishima, in the middle of Lake Shintai, is now Ariyasuba Myojin Shrine, this is it." The "Yasuba Myojin Shrine" which the "Hyōchū Kofudoki" identifies with "Chomiya" is thought to refer to the present-day Ojima Shrine. Ojima Shrine enshrines Onamuchino-mikoto (another name for Okuninushi-no-mikoto) as its main deity, and within the shrine grounds there is a stone monument commemorating the site of the "Chomiya" shrine. The "Osugi Myojin" of Yasuba village is thought to refer to the current Osugi Shrine.
=== Founded === It is said to have been founded in the first year of [[Jingo-keiun|the Jingo Keiun]] era ( 767 ).
The "Osugi Shrine Brief History" states that the monk [[:ja:勝道|Shodo]] visited the area, which was suffering from an epidemic, on his way to [[Nikkō|Nikko]] in [[Shimotsuke Province]] . He used the giant cedar as [[Himorogi|a sacred tree]] to enslave '''[[Ōmiwa Shrine|Miwa Myojin]]''' (Okami Shrine) and performed numerous miracles to save the people, which is why the shrine came to be worshiped as the "Anbasama of Demon Barae" <ref>「あんば」とは、当時入り海であった霞ケ浦に突き出た半島を「安婆島」と呼んでおり、その地に大杉神社が作られたことに由来する</ref> <ref>{{Citation|last=柳正博|title=利根川の水神信仰|date=3月|volume=2|pages=82|year=1989|series=調査研究報告|publisher=埼玉県立さきたま資料館|和書}}</ref> . The history of the Inashiki branch of the Ibaraki Prefecture [[:ja:神社庁|Shrine Association]] states, "Seeing that the villagers were suffering greatly from the epidemic, he took pity on them and performed a ritual to appease the Omiwa-no-Okami of Yamato Province under a large cedar tree, and the villagers immediately made a full recovery." However, regarding the sacred object, there are sources which say that it is not the giant cedar itself, but the "spiritual deity Fudo Myo-o" carved by the monk Shotodo, such as "It is Fudo Myo-o, the spiritual deity who subdues demons, carved by the monk Shotodo during the Jingo Keiun era" (Tonegawa Zushi) and "The sacred object is the spiritual deity Fudo Myo-o, the spiritual deity who subdues demons, carved by the monk Shotodo during the Jingo Keiun era" (Jozan Sosui).
In the 15th year [[Enryaku|of the Enryaku era]] (796) or in May of the same year (Inashiki County Local History), Kaiken Ajari of [[:ja:延暦寺|Enryaku-ji]] Temple prayed at Osugi Shrine for the surrender of [[:ja:悪路王|King Akujo]] (Takamaru). The [[:ja:利根川図志|Tonegawa Zushi]] states, "Dengyo Daishi himself came to this place begging for a statue of [[Maitreya|Acala]], who subdues the four demons, which he had carved himself, and after a spiritual dream he enshrined it here, just like Osugi Daimyojin. He also enshrined the statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva, made by Konsuji Katsukura from [[:ja:天竺|India]], thus founding a sacred temple and naming it Ryukozan An'on-ji." It says that he enshrined the "Acala, who subdues the four demons," made by Dengyo Daishi ( [[:ja:最澄|Saicho]] ), along with the "Osugi Daimyojin (spiritual deity Acala)," and further established Ryukozan [[安穏寺 (結城市)|An'on-ji]] with the "statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva," made by Konsuji Katsukura from India, as the principal image. As a reward for his prayers for peace in the nation, he was granted a sacred land, and according to the Inashiki branch, a shrine to "Osugi Daimyojin" was subsequently constructed within the grounds of An'on-ji Temple.
The shrine's website states that An'on-ji Temple was founded in 805 .
The New Compilation of Hitachi Kokushi states, "There is a shrine to Osugi Myojin within the temple grounds. Although this shrine was built later, people from far and wide revered it so much that over time, a shrine building was constructed, and as a result, this temple has become truly like [[:ja:別当寺|a beneficiary]] ." It states that originally there was An'on-ji Temple, and later Osugi Myojin was enshrined there as a shrine within the temple grounds, but the roles of master and servant were reversed due to the extreme reverence. This corresponds to the description in the Inashiki branch, which says that the temple was granted a sacred land in recognition of its meritorious efforts at praying for peace for the nation, centered around Ryukazan An'on-ji Temple, and that "Osugi Daimyojin" was later constructed within the temple grounds. It is possible that Osugi Daimyojin had been worshiped even before that, without having a shrine building.
=== Middle Ages === The Tonegawa Zushi from [[Genryaku|the Genryaku]] and [[Bunji (era)|Bun'ichi]] eras (1184-1190) states, "Osugi Daimyojin resented the rampage of the Taira [[Taira clan|clan]] and appeared as Hitachibo Kaison, who assisted Judge Minamoto no Yoshitsune in defeating the Taira clan. After his success, he returned to this place and carved a statue of himself, which he presented to Osugi Palace." There is a legend that Hitachibo Kaison was [[Incarnation|an incarnation]] of Osugi Daimyojin or [[Shinshi|a divine messenger]] (attachment). On September 27, 1189, he disappeared suddenly on a rainbow of colorful clouds, and "people came to know that Kaisonbo was an associate of the great deity" (Osugi Myojin Ryaku Engi). In the past, an annual festival was held on September 27th, the day Hitachibo Kaison disappeared.
In 1241, [[Ninji|the]] Jozan Sosui records that "a branch of the spirit of Imamiya Shrine in Murasakino, Kyoto was enshrined and the shrine was renamed Imamiya Osugi Daigongen," and the two '''deities Okuninushi no Mikoto''' and '''Sukunahikona no Mikoto''' were [[:ja:分霊|enshrined]] together from [[:ja:今宮神社_(京都市)|Imamiya Shrine]] in [[:ja:京都|Kyoto]] .
During [[Ōnin War|the Onin War]] (1467-1477), the temple's land was plundered, but during [[Keichō|the Keicho]] era (1596-1615), [[Tokugawa shogunate|the Tokugawa shogunate]] granted An'on-ji Temple a fief of 20 koku (Shinpen Hitachi Kokushi) and [[:ja:朱印状|a red seal]] exempting it from various taxes. Additionally, the Tonegawa Scenic Spot Guide states, "The monk [[:ja:天海|Tenkai]] of Mt. Hiei was ordered to take on the role of betto priest concurrently, and from then on all shrine affairs at Annon- [[:ja:寛永寺|ji were handled by Toei-zan]] ," and the temple came under the control of Toei-zan Kan'ei-ji.
Regarding Tenkai's achievements, the "Brief History of Osugi Shrine" states, "Tenkai floated a boat in Tojo Bay and invited Osugi Daimyojin, who is enshrined to the east of the bay, to visit him. He performed a ritual that made it rain beautifully, and performed a miracle." "He designated this shrine as the guardian shrine of the evil spirits direction of [[Edo Castle]], and became the chief priest of his own betto An'on-ji temple." "Due to Tenkai's connection with this shrine, Betto An'on-ji temple became a direct affiliated temple of [[:ja:輪王寺|Nikkozan Rinnoji temple]] ." The information board within the shrine grounds also says that the Osugi no Okami that Tenkai enshrined when he prayed for rain was a "dragon god."
* Tenkai (Zuifu) was invited by [[:ja:蘆名義広|Ashina Yoshihiro]], who became the lord of Edosaki Castle, and served as the chief priest of Edosaki Fudoin Temple from [[Tenshō (Momoyama period)|1570]] to 1603. During this time, there is an anecdote that in [[Bunroku|1594]], in response to a plea from the people of [[Hitachi Province]], who were suffering from a drought, he prayed for [[Rain dance|rain]] . When Tenkai was about to pray for rain at Takada Bay, a girl appeared from the shade of a willow tree and handed him [[:ja:金剛杵|a five-pronged vajra]] (five-pronged vajra) to use in the prayer, then left. As she prayed for rain, lightning flashed from the five-pronged vajra and the image of [[:ja:文殊菩薩|Manjusri Bodhisattva]] riding [[Lion|a lion]] appeared for a moment, and he realized that his daughter was an incarnation of Manjusri Bodhisattva. The people who were saved from the drought expressed their gratitude to Manjusri Bodhisattva and praised Tenkai's virtues. This rain-making story is also recorded in the "History of the Founder of Mount Toei, Jigen Daishi" . Osugi Shrine does not appear to appear in these tales. * The New Compilation of Hitachi Kokushi describes Annon-ji Temple as "a Tendai sect temple, a branch of Ono Hozen-ji Temple, and known as Ryuge-san Jison-in Temple," and according to [[:ja:本末制度|the branch temple system]], it was a branch temple of [[:ja:逢善寺|Hozen-ji Temple]] in Ono, Inashiki City.
In 1725 (the 10th year of the [[Kyōhō|Kyoho]] era), the "Demon-Exorcising Music" began, and as it spread, worship of him as a god for warding off [[smallpox]] and for water traffic spread throughout the Kanto region and the [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific]] coast of Tohoku. Its origins date back to [[Genna|1617]], when Genba Tanaka (the founder of [[:ja:ヒゲタ醤油|Higeta Soy Sauce]] ) brought it from [[Kii Province|Kishu]] along with the Twelve Seats Kagura dance. There is an entry for “Anbasama (Awa-sama)” in the Daijisen Digital [[:ja:大辞泉|Dictionary]], which describes it as “a god worshipped in fishing villages along the Pacific coast from Chiba Prefecture to the Tohoku region."
In 1778, the sacred tree, Taro Cedar, was burned down.
In 1798, both the [[Kansei|shrine]] and temple were destroyed by fire.
[[Kyōwa|In]] 1802, a fire broke out again.
In [[Bunka|1813]], following repeated fires, "the difficulty of restoration reached the attention of Imperial Princess Kinen, the 9th abbot of Rinno-ji Temple, who bestowed 1,000 ryo of gold" (Inashiki County Local History), and "the current shrine building was constructed with the 1,000 ryo of gold that [[:ja:一品親王|the first rank prince]] bestowed on it" (Inashiki Branch), and the shrine was rebuilt. Shortly afterwards, in the Bunsei 12th year (1815), the Sojo Nikki recorded that "Osugi Myojin is said to be the name of Hitachibo Kaison, and although the shrine grounds are modern, it is very lively. (There is also an Osugi shrine in Kashima.)" (Dai Nippon Chimei Jisho). The relocation took place in Bunka 13 (1816) .
=== After the Meiji Period === After [[Meiji Restoration|the Meiji Restoration]], due to the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, Annon-ji Temple was abolished and turned into [[Shinto shrine|a shrine office]] .
On [[Meiji period|November]] 14, 1871, Niiharu Prefecture was established as a result of the first merger of prefectures, and the Niiharu Prefectural Central Teaching Institute was established at Osugi Shrine ("A Brief History of Osugi Shrine").
In October 1873, it was ranked as a village shrine. By the way, in the "Photographic Album of Ibaraki Prefecture Shrines" published in [[Shōwa period|1942]], it was a village shrine, but in the Shrine Details Database held by the National Institute of Japanese Literature, it has been promoted to a village shrine.
On May 7, 1875, Ibaraki Prefecture was established as a result of the second merger of prefectures.
In 1878, An'on-ji Temple was rebuilt.
In April 1907, it merged with the unranked Ise Shrine ( [[Amaterasu|Dainichikagamine]] ) in [[:ja:阿波村_(茨城県)|Awa Village]] .
On January 31, 1978, “Anba-bayashi” was designated [[:ja:記録作成等の措置を講ずべき無形の民俗文化財|an intangible folk cultural property for which measures such as recording are required]] .
In 1982, it became a specially designated shrine under the Shinto Shrines Association.
Construction and repair work began in [[Heisei period|1996]] as part of the Heisei Great Construction Project.
Restoration work on the shrine building (Osugiden) was completed in 2006.

=== Katsuma Shrine === Katsuma Shrine is located in the southeast of the temple grounds. The enshrined deity is unknown.
Its ancient name was "Magisha" and it has its own ancient history. "Bareki" means the joists of a stable (the cross beams that support the floorboards), and by extension refers to a manger or the stable itself. "Umatakagami" is the guardian deity of horses and is also known as "Umayanokami" ( [[:ja:厩神|stable god]] ), and is a part of folk beliefs in various regions.
[[Heian period|During the Heian period]], Shinda Horse Ranch (mentioned in [[Engishiki|the Engishiki]] ) was located in Shinda [[:ja:美浦村|, Miho Village]], one of the various [[:ja:諸国牧|ranches]] in Hitachi Province (ranches under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Military Affairs), and [[Jōgan|a shrine]] was established there in 862 to protect the horses. When the horse pasture was abolished at the end of the Heian period, it was passed through Koda [[:ja:稲敷市|in Inashiki City]], and then moved to the grounds of Osugi Shrine during the Kamakura period. There used to be a horse racing track behind Annon-ji Temple (Okuyama), where horse races were held until the early [[Shōwa period|Showa]] period. The stone shrine was enshrined in a place overlooking the track. With the disappearance of farm horses, the shrine was forgotten, but in 2002 a shrine building was constructed on the same site and the shrine was moved there .
Currently, people from [[:ja:日本中央競馬会|the Japan]] Racing Association (JRA) [[:ja:美浦トレーニングセンター|Miho Training Center]], which is located on the site of the ancient Shinta Horse Ranch, come to offer [[Prayer|prayers]] for the year, along with those from the headquarters. It is also well known among horse racing fans. Incidentally, [[:ja:神馬|the sacred horse]] currently used in the Osugi Shrine festival is borrowed from the Miho Training Center because the farmer no longer has any horses left. Many horseshoes have been donated in front of the shrine, and there are also rare charms such as "winning horse charms," "horseshoe votive plaques," and "mane charms."

Ōsugi Shrine (Ōsugi Jinja) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Aba, Inashiki City, [[Ibaraki Prefecture]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Osugi Shrine {{!}} Visit {{!}} IBARAKI GUIDE|url=https://visit.ibarakiguide.jp/en/sightseeing/22351/|access-date=2024-03-29|website=visit.ibarakiguide.jp|language=en-US}}</ref> It is known as the "[[Nikkō Tōshō-gū]] of [[Ibaraki Prefecture|Ibaraki]]" due to its lavish shrine buildings and is affectionately called "Anba-sama." The shrine has historically been known by names such as Ōsugi Dai-myōjin, Ōsugi Daigongen, and Imamiya Ōsugi Dai-myōjin. The [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|former shrine ranking]] was a village shrine. It is currently designated as a "[[Beppyo shrine|Beppyo Jinja]]" by the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. It serves as the head shrine for about 670 Ōsugi Shrines distributed across the [[Kantō region|Kantō]] and [[Tōhoku region|Tōhoku regions]].
== Deities Worshiped == [[File:Osugi-shrine_festival,Inashiki-city,Japan.jpg|right|thumb|254x254px| Awa floats at the Osugi Shrine festival]]
;Main deity : [[Yamato Okunitama|Yamato]] [[Ōmononushi|Omononushi Kushimikatama]] no Mikoto ; Enshrined : [[Ōkuninushi|Okuninushi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Sukunabikona|Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto]]
Initially, the shrine enshrined Yamato Ōmono Nushi Kushi Mikatama no Mikoto from Ōmiya Shrine in Yamato Province. In 1241, [[Ōkuninushi|Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] and [[Sukunabikona|Sukunahikona no Mikoto]] were also enshrined from {{ill|10=ja|11=今宮神社_(京都市)|Imamiya Shrine|en}}. The configuration of deities mirrors that of [[Ōmiwa Shrine|Ōmiya Shrine]]. The shrine's name derives from a large [[Cryptomeria japonica]] tree within its grounds, originally part of a trio of cedars named Tarōsugi, Jirōsugi, and Saburōsugi, though Tarōsugi was destroyed by fire in 1778.
The shrine is also associated with the tengu, mythical creatures in Japanese folklore, specifically the "Hana-taka Tengu" and "Karasu Tengu." During the Bunji era (1185-1189), a retainer of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitsune|en}} named {{ill|10=ja|11=常陸坊海尊|Hitachibō Kaison}} performed various miracles attributed to the divine virtue of the great cedar. This led to the belief that prayers made through Kaison would be fulfilled by the great cedar deity. Kaison, resembling a tengu, helped establish the tengu belief through his image, leading to the recognition of Hana-taka Tengu and Karasu Tengu as guardian deities. Hana-taka Tengu is known as the "Wish-fulfilling Tengu," and Karasu Tengu as the "Granting Tengu," believed to bestow blessings and fulfill wishes.
It worships a rarely worshipped [[kami]] named Anba sama.<ref name=":0" />

== History == According to the shrine's website, the area of "Anba" belonged to the ancient [[kuni no miyatsuko]] system before the Ritsuryō system, being part of the Uda Province. Ōsugi Shrine was the most important shrine venerating the {{ill|10=ja|11=下海上国造|Ukami kuni no miyatsuko}}.
In ancient times, the Awa region, part of the plateau where the shrine is located, protruded into the seas called "Shinoda Ryūkai" (west coast of [[Lake Kasumigaura]]) and "Enoura Ryūkai" (an inland sea that spread out in the lowlands of the Tone River basin). Awa was positioned deeply within an inland bay surrounded by Awasaki and Sugatsu, and a large cedar there was worshipped by fishermen and served as a navigational landmark for ships sailing the internal sea (Katori Inner Sea or Jōsō Inner Sea).
=== "Norihama" and "Abanoshi Island" === In the {{ill|10=ja|11=常陸国風土記|Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}}, place names that are thought to refer to the Awa region include "Norihama" in the section on Shinoda County and "Aba no Shima" in the section on Namegata County.
" '''Norihama''' " 「'''乗濱'''」appears in the description of "Norimano Village" in the section on {{ill|10=ja|11=信太郡|Shinoda County}}. When {{ill|10=ja|11=ヤマトタケル|Emperor Yamato Takeru}} was touring the coast and came to Norihama, he saw that there were many people drying seaweed in Hamaura, so the village came to be called "Norimahama." Also, to the east of Norihama-sato is Ukishima-mura, which is surrounded by sea on all sides, and the farmers there made their living by producing salt.
" '''Aba no Shima''' " 「'''安婆之島'''」appears in the description of Takekazama no Mikoto's view of the country in the section on {{ill|10=ja|11=行方郡_(茨城県)|Namegata County}}. Takekarima no Mikoto was camping on "Abanoshi Island" and saw smoke in a bay far in the eastern sea. He made a vow that if it was the smoke of a heavenly being, he would cover him, but if it was the smoke of bandits, he would let it drift into the sea. When the smoke shot out to sea and drifted away, he realized that a vicious bandit (Kunisu) was there. After Takeshikamado murdered Kunisu, the place where it was said he would kill him painfully became "Itakunogo," the place where it was said he would kill him normally became "Butsunanomura," the place where it was said he would kill him cheaply became "Abakinosato," and the place where it was said he would kill him well became "Yoshimaenomura." According to the "Hyōchū Kofudoki," "Itaku" is "Itako," "Futsuna" is "Furutaka," "Abari" is "Awadai" in Furutaka, and "Yoshizaki" is "Ezaki" in {{ill|10=ja|11=延方村|Nobukata village}}, all of which became place names in {{ill|10=ja|11=潮来市|Itako City}}, located across from "Aba Island."
Awa belonged to "Takada-go" (Shinpen Hitachi Kokushi) or "Norihama-go" ({{ill|10=ja|11=大日本地名辞書|Dai Nippon Chimei Jisho}}) mentioned in the "{{ill|10=ja|11=和名類聚抄|Wamyo Ruijusho}}". The New Hitachi Kokushikan states, "In ancient times, the southwestern part of this town was entirely covered with reeds and a land of deep mud, while the northeastern part was, as it is today, a flowing sea, so it was really like a single island. What was once called Abana Island was probably the area of the two towns of Takada and Norihama (this can be known from the current names of Yasuba Village, Awazaki Village, etc.)."
It states that the two towns of Takada and Norihama were the "Aba no Shima" and "Norihama" mentioned in the Hitachi Koku Fudoki. Even today, the area from Isazu to Sugazu in Inashiki City is a peninsula-like or island-like plateau. Regarding the description of Namegata County, it says, "It is said that one crossed the inland sea from Ababa Island to Itarai. The present-day Awazaki and Itarai are opposite each other and are in the same direction, so there is no doubt that what is referred to as Ababa Island here is the area of Takada and Norihama," and the place where Takekashima no Mikoto looked into the country is stated to be "Awazaki." The Great Japanese Place Name Dictionary states, "The Ababa Island mentioned in the Kofudoki probably corresponds to the corresponding Ukishima Island or Awazaki," and the Annotated Kofudoki states, "This so-called Ababa Island is probably the location of Ukishima Island. Now, on Ukishima Island, there is Aba Myojin Shrine, where the deity worshipped is Okuninushi no Mikoto. Aba Village is also worshipped, and the local name is Osugi Myojin." These are some of the views that it is a "floating island."
Incidentally, the note in the "Hyōchū Kofudoki" states that there is an "Yaba Myojin Shrine" on Ukishima, and an "Osugi Myojin Shrine" in Yaba village which enshrines the same deity. Regarding "Yasuba Myojin Shrine," the note in the separate description of "Ukishima no Chomiya" also states, "Ukishima, in the middle of Lake Shintai, is now Ariyasuba Myojin Shrine, this is it." The "Yasuba Myojin Shrine" which the "Hyōchū Kofudoki" identifies with "Chomiya" is thought to refer to the present-day Ojima Shrine. Ojima Shrine enshrines Onamuchino-mikoto (another name for Okuninushi-no-mikoto) as its main deity, and within the shrine grounds there is a stone monument commemorating the site of the "Chomiya" shrine. The "Osugi Myojin" of Yasuba village is thought to refer to the current Osugi Shrine.
=== Founded === It is said to have been founded in the first year of [[Jingo-keiun|the Jingo Keiun]] era (767).
The "Osugi Shrine Brief History" states that the monk {{ill|10=ja|11=勝道|Shodo}} visited the area, which was suffering from an epidemic, on his way to [[Nikkō|Nikko]] in [[Shimotsuke Province]]. He used the giant cedar as [[Himorogi|a sacred tree]] to enslave '''[[Ōmiwa Shrine|Miwa Myojin]]''' (Okami Shrine) and performed numerous miracles to save the people, which is why the shrine came to be worshiped as the "Anbasama of Demon Barae" <ref>「あんば」とは、当時入り海であった霞ケ浦に突き出た半島を「安婆島」と呼んでおり、その地に大杉神社が作られたことに由来する</ref> <ref>{{Citation|last=柳正博|title=利根川の水神信仰|date=3月|volume=2|pages=82|year=1989|series=調査研究報告|publisher=埼玉県立さきたま資料館|和書}}</ref>. The history of the Inashiki branch of the Ibaraki Prefecture {{ill|10=ja|11=神社庁|Shrine Association}} states, "Seeing that the villagers were suffering greatly from the epidemic, he took pity on them and performed a ritual to appease the Omiwa-no-Okami of Yamato Province under a large cedar tree, and the villagers immediately made a full recovery." However, regarding the sacred object, there are sources which say that it is not the giant cedar itself, but the "spiritual deity Fudo Myo-o" carved by the monk Shotodo, such as "It is Fudo Myo-o, the spiritual deity who subdues demons, carved by the monk Shotodo during the Jingo Keiun era" (Tonegawa Zushi) and "The
sacred object is the spiritual deity Fudo Myo-o, the spiritual deity who subdues demons, carved by the monk Shotodo during the Jingo Keiun era" (Jozan Sosui).
In the 15th year [[Enryaku|of the Enryaku era]] (796) or in May of the same year (Inashiki County Local History), Kaiken Ajari of {{ill|10=ja|11=延暦寺|Enryaku-ji}} Temple prayed at Osugi Shrine for the surrender of {{ill|10=ja|11=悪路王|King Akujo}} (Takamaru). The {{ill|10=ja|11=利根川図志|Tonegawa Zushi}} states, "Dengyo Daishi himself came to this place begging for a statue of [[Maitreya|Acala]], who subdues the four demons, which he had carved himself, and after a spiritual dream he enshrined it here, just like Osugi Daimyojin. He also enshrined the statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva, made by Konsuji Katsukura from {{ill|10=ja|11=天竺|India}}, thus founding a sacred temple and naming it Ryukozan {{ill|10=ja|11=安穏寺 (結城市)|An'on-ji}}." It says that he enshrined the "Acala, who subdues the four demons," made by Dengyo Daishi ({{ill|10=ja|11=最澄|Saicho}}), along with the "Osugi Daimyojin (spiritual deity Acala)," and further established Ryukozan {{ill|10=ja|11=安穏寺|An'on-ji}} with the "statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva," made by Konsuji Katsukura from India, as the principal image. As a reward for his prayers for peace in the nation, he was granted a sacred land, and according to the Inashiki branch, a shrine to "Osugi Daimyojin" was subsequently constructed within the grounds of An'on-ji Temple.
The shrine's website states that An'on-ji Temple was founded in 805.
The New Compilation of Hitachi Kokushi states, "There is a shrine to Osugi Myojin within the temple grounds. Although this shrine was built later, people from far and wide revered it so much that over time, a shrine building was constructed, and as a result, this temple has become truly like {{ill|10=ja|11=別当寺|a beneficiary}}." It states that originally there was An'on-ji Temple, and later Osugi Myojin was enshrined there as a shrine within the temple grounds, but the roles of master and servant were reversed due to the extreme reverence. This corresponds to the description in the Inashiki branch, which says that the temple was granted a sacred land in recognition of its meritorious efforts at praying for peace for the nation, centered around Ryukazan An'on-ji Temple, and that "Osugi Daimyojin" was later constructed within the temple grounds. It is possible that Osugi Daimyojin had been worshiped even before that, without having a shrine building.
=== Middle Ages === The Tonegawa Zushi from [[Genryaku|the Genryaku]] and [[Bunji (era)|Bun'ichi]] eras (1184-1190) states, "Osugi Daimyojin resented the rampage of the Taira [[Taira clan|clan]] and appeared as Hitachibo Kaison, who assisted Judge Minamoto no Yoshitsune in defeating the Taira clan. After his success, he returned to this place and carved a statue of himself, which he presented to Osugi Palace." There is a legend that Hitachibo Kaison was [[Incarnation|an incarnation]] of Osugi Daimyojin or [[Shinshi|a divine messenger]] (attachment). On September 27, 1189, he disappeared suddenly on a rainbow of colorful clouds, and "people came to know that Kaisonbo was an associate of the great deity" (Osugi Myojin Ryaku Engi). In the past, an annual festival was held on September 27th, the day Hitachibo Kaison disappeared.
In 1241, the Jozan Sosui records that "a branch of the spirit of Imamiya Shrine in Murasakino, Kyoto was enshrined and the shrine was renamed Imamiya Osugi Daigongen," and the two '''deities Okuninushi no Mikoto''' and '''Sukunah
ikona no Mikoto''' were {{ill|10=ja|11=分霊|enshrined}} together from {{ill|10=ja|11=今宮神社_(京都市)|Imamiya Shrine}} in {{ill|10=ja|11=京都|Kyoto}}.
During {{ill|10=ja|11=応仁の乱|the Onin War}} (1467-1477), the temple's land was plundered, but during {{ill|10=ja|11=慶長|the Keicho}} era (1596-1615), {{ill|10=ja|11=徳川幕府|the Tokugawa shogunate}} granted An'on-ji Temple a fief of 20 koku (Shinpen Hitachi Kokushi) and {{ill|10=ja|11=朱印状|a red seal}} exempting it from various taxes. Additionally, the Tonegawa Scenic Spot Guide states, "The monk {{ill|10=ja|11=天海|Tenkai}} of Mt. Hiei was ordered to take on the role of betto priest concurrently, and from then on all shrine affairs at Annon-{{ill|10=ja|11=寛永寺|ji}} were handled by Toei-zan," and the temple came under the control of Toei-zan Kan'ei-ji.
Regarding Tenkai's achievements, the "Brief History of Osugi Shrine" states, "Tenkai floated a boat in Tojo Bay and invited Osugi Daimyojin, who is enshrined to the east of the bay, to visit him. He performed a ritual that made it rain beautifully, and performed a miracle." "He designated this shrine as the guardian shrine of the evil spirits direction of [[Edo Castle]], and became the chief priest of his own betto An'on-ji temple." "Due to Tenkai's connection with this shrine, Betto An'on-ji temple became a direct affiliated temple of {{ill|10=ja|11=輪王寺|Nikkozan Rinnoji temple}}." The information board within the shrine grounds also says that the Osugi no Okami that Tenkai enshrined when he prayed for rain was a "dragon god."
* Tenkai (Zuifu) was invited by {{ill|10=ja|11=蘆名義広|Ashina Yoshihiro}}, who became the lord of Edosaki Castle, and served as the chief priest of Edosaki Fudoin Temple from {{ill|10=ja|11=天正_(桃山時代)|1570}} to 1603. During this time, there is an anecdote that in {{ill|10=ja|11=文禄|1594}}, in response to a plea from the people of {{ill|10=ja|11=常陸国|Hitachi Province}}, who were suffering from a drought, he prayed for {{ill|10=ja|11=雨乞い|rain}}. When Tenkai was about to pray for rain at Takada Bay, a girl appeared from the shade of a willow tree and handed him {{ill|10=ja|11=金剛杵|a five-pronged vajra}} (five-pronged vajra) to use in the prayer, then left. As she prayed for rain, lightning flashed from the five-pronged vajra and the image of {{ill|10=ja|11=文殊菩薩|Manjusri Bodhisattva}} riding {{ill|10=ja|11=獅子|a lion}} appeared for a moment, and he realized that his daughter was an incarnation of Manjusri Bodhisattva. The people who were saved from the drought expressed their gratitude to Manjusri Bodhisattva and praised Tenkai's virtues. This rain-making story is also recorded in the "History of the Founder of Mount Toei, Jigen Daishi" . Osugi Shrine does not appear to appear in these tales. * The New Compilation of Hitachi Kokushi describes Annon-ji Temple as "a Tendai sect temple, a branch of Ono Hozen-ji Temple, and known as Ryuge-san Jison-in Temple," and according to {{ill|10=ja|11=本末制度|the branch temple system}}, it was a branch temple of {{ill|10=ja|11=逢善寺|Hozen-ji Temple}} in Ono, Inashiki City.
In 1725 (the 10th year of the {{ill|10=
ja|11=享保|Kyoho}} era), the "Demon-Exorcising Music" began, and as it spread, worship of him as a god for warding off {{ill|10=ja|11=疱疹|smallpox}} and for water traffic spread throughout the Kanto region and the {{ill|10=ja|11=太平洋|Pacific}} coast of Tohoku. Its origins date back to {{ill|10=ja|11=元和|1617}}, when Genba Tanaka (the founder of {{ill|10=ja|11=ヒゲタ醤油|Higeta Soy Sauce}}) brought it from {{ill|10=ja|11=紀伊国|Kishu}} along with the Twelve Seats Kagura dance. There is an entry for “Anbasama (Awa-sama)” in the Daijisen Digital {{ill|10=ja|11=大辞泉|Dictionary}}, which describes it as “a god worshipped in fishing villages along the Pacific coast from Chiba Prefecture to the Tohoku region."
In 1778, the sacred tree, Taro Cedar, was burned down.
In 1798, both the {{ill|10=ja|11=寛政|shrine}} and temple were destroyed by fire.
{{ill|10=ja|11=享和|In}} 1802, a fire broke out again.
In {{ill|10=ja|11=文化_(年号)|1813}}, following repeated fires, "the difficulty of restoration reached the attention of Imperial Princess Kinen, the 9th abbot of Rinno-ji Temple, who bestowed 1,000 ryo of gold" (Inashiki County Local History), and "the current shrine building was constructed with the 1,000 ryo of gold that {{ill|10=ja|11=一品親王|the first rank prince}} bestowed on it" (Inashiki Branch), and the shrine was rebuilt. Shortly afterwards, in the Bunsei 12th year (1815), the Sojo Nikki recorded that "Osugi Myojin is said to be the name of Hitachibo Kaison, and although the shrine grounds are modern, it is very lively. (There is also an Osugi shrine in Kashima.)" (Dai Nippon Chimei Jisho). The relocation took place in Bunka 13 (1816) .
=== After the Meiji Period === After {{ill|10=ja|11=明治維新|the Meiji Restoration}}, due to the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, Annon-ji Temple was abolished and turned into {{ill|10=ja|11=神社|a shrine office}}.
On {{ill|10=ja|11=明治時代|November}} 14, 1871, Niiharu Prefecture was established as a result of the first merger of prefectures, and the Niiharu Prefectural Central Teaching Institute was established at Osugi Shrine ("A Brief History of Osugi Shrine").
In October 1873, it was ranked as a village shrine. By the way, in the "Photographic Album of Ibaraki Prefecture Shrines" published in {{ill|10=ja|11=昭和時代|1942}}, it was a village shrine, but in the Shrine Details Database held by the National Institute of Japanese Literature, it has been promoted to a village shrine.
On May 7, 1875, Ibaraki Prefecture was established as a result of the second merger of prefectures.
In 1878, An'on-ji Temple was rebuilt.
In April 1907, it merged with the unranked Ise Shrine ({{ill|10=ja|11=天照大神|Dainichikagamine}}) in {{ill|10=ja|11=阿波村_(茨城県)|Awa Village}}.
On January 31, 1978, “Anba-bayashi” was designated {{ill|10=ja|11=記録作成等の措置を講ずべき無形の民俗文化財|an intangible folk cultural property for which measures such as recording are required}}.
In 1982, it became a specially designated shrine under the Shinto Shrines Association.
Construction and repair work began in {{ill|10=ja|11=平成時代|1996}} as part of the Heisei Great Construction Project.
Restoration work on the shrine building (Osugiden) was completed in 2006.
== Shrine grounds == The names of the enshrined deities are listed on explanatory boards within the temple grounds.
* A shrine located in the northwest of the temple grounds.
: Deities enshrined at '''Okuni Shrine''' : [[Ōkuninushi|Okuninushi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Kotoshironushi]] -no- : '''Deity of Ise Shrine''' - [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Omikami]] : '''Hakusan Shrine''' Deity [[:ja:菊理媛神|-Kikurihime]] : Deities worshipped at '''the four shrines''' - [[:ja:カミムスビ|Ame-no-]] [[Ame-no-Minakanushi|Minaka-nushi, Takami-]] [[:ja:タカミムスビ|musubi-no-Kami, Kami-musubi-no-Kami,]] [[Amaterasu]] [[:ja:神直日神|-Omikami, Kaminao-no-Kami,]] and [[:ja:直毘神|O-nao-no-Kami]] : '''Tenmangu Shrine''' Deity - [[Sugawara no Michizane]]
* A shrine located in the southeast of the temple grounds.
: '''[[:ja:大杉神社|Inari Shrine]]''' (Shoichii Ryūshin Sōsei Saisho Inari Daimyojin) Deity - Ukemome : '''Deity of Katsuma''' Shrine - Unknown : '''Aioi Shrine'''
* The Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Photo Album lists three shrines as follows: Inari Shrine (Ukemochi no Mikoto), Hakusan Shrine (Kukurihime no Mikoto), and Okuni Shrine (Onamochi no Mikoto, Sukunahikona no Mikoto). * The Inashiki branch of the Ibaraki Prefectural Shrine Association has four shrines: Inari Shrine, Hakusan Shrine, Okuni Shrine, and Isose Shrine.
=== Katsuma Shrine === Katsuma Shrine is located in the southeast of the temple grounds. The enshrined deity is unknown.
Its ancient name was "Magisha" and it has its own ancient history. "Bareki" means the joists of a stable (the cross beams that support the floorboards), and by extension refers to a manger or the stable itself. "Umatakagami" is the guardian deity of horses and is also known as "Umayanokami" ( [[:ja:厩神|stable god]] ), and is a part of folk beliefs in various regions.
[[Heian period|During the Heian period]], Shinda Horse Ranch (mentioned in [[Engishiki|the Engishiki]] ) was located in Shinda [[:ja:美浦村|, Miho Village]], one of the various [[:ja:諸国牧|ranches]] in Hitachi Province (ranches under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Military Affairs), and [[Jōgan|a shrine]] was established there in 862 to protect the horses. When the horse pasture was abolished at the end of the Heian period, it was passed through Koda [[:ja:稲敷市|in Inashiki City]], and then moved to the grounds of Osugi Shrine during the Kamakura period. There used to be a horse racing track behind Annon-ji Temple (Okuyama), where horse races were held until the early [[Shōwa period|Showa]] period. The stone shrine was enshrined in a place overlooking the track. With the disappearance of farm horses, the shrine was forgotten, but in 2002 a shrine building was constructed on the same site and the shrine was moved there .
Currently, people from [[:ja:日本中央競馬会|the Japan]] Racing Association (JRA) [[:ja:美浦トレーニングセンター|Miho Training Center]], which is located on the site of the ancient Shinta Horse Ranch, come to offer [[Prayer|prayers]] for the year, along with those from the headquarters. It is also well known among horse racing fans. Incidentally, [[:ja:神馬|the sacred horse]] currently used in the Osugi Shrine festival is borrowed from the Miho Training Center because the farmer no longer has any horses left. Many horseshoes have been donated in front of the shrine, and there are also rare charms such as "winning horse charms," "horseshoe votive plaques," and "mane charms."

Ōsugi Shrine (Ōsugi Jinja) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Aba, Inashiki City, [[Ibaraki Prefecture]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Osugi Shrine {{!}} Visit {{!}} IBARAKI GUIDE|url=https://visit.ibarakiguide.jp/en/sightseeing/22351/|access-date=2024-03-29|website=visit.ibarakiguide.jp|language=en-US}}</ref> It is known as the "[[Nikkō Tōshō-gū]] of [[Ibaraki Prefecture|Ibaraki]]" due to its lavish shrine buildings and is affectionately called "Anba-sama." The shrine has historically been known by names such as Ōsugi Dai-myōjin, Ōsugi Daigongen, and Imamiya Ōsugi Dai-myōjin. The [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|former shrine ranking]] was a village shrine. It is currently designated as a "[[Beppyo shrine|Beppyo Jinja]]" by the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. It serves as the head shrine for about 670 Ōsugi Shrines distributed across the [[Kantō region|Kantō]] and [[Tōhoku region|Tōhoku regions]].
== Deities Worshiped == [[File:Osugi-shrine_festival,Inashiki-city,Japan.jpg|right|thumb|254x254px| Awa floats at the Osugi Shrine festival]]
;Main deity : [[Yamato Okunitama|Yamato]] [[Ōmononushi|Omononushi Kushimikatama]] no Mikoto ; Enshrined : [[Ōkuninushi|Okuninushi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Sukunabikona|Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto]]
Initially, the shrine enshrined Yamato Ōmono Nushi Kushi Mikatama no Mikoto from Ōmiya Shrine in Yamato Province. In 1241, [[Ōkuninushi|Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] and [[Sukunabikona|Sukunahikona no Mikoto]] were also enshrined from {{ill|10=ja|11=今宮神社_(京都市)|Imamiya Shrine|en}}. The configuration of deities mirrors that of [[Ōmiwa Shrine|Ōmiya Shrine]]. The shrine's name derives from a large [[Cryptomeria japonica]] tree within its grounds, originally part of a trio of cedars named Tarōsugi, Jirōsugi, and Saburōsugi, though Tarōsugi was destroyed by fire in 1778.
The shrine is also associated with the tengu, mythical creatures in Japanese folklore, specifically the "Hana-taka Tengu" and "Karasu Tengu." During the Bunji era (1185-1189), a retainer of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitsune|en}} named {{ill|10=ja|11=常陸坊海尊|Hitachibō Kaison}} performed various miracles attributed to the divine virtue of the great cedar. This led to the belief that prayers made through Kaison would be fulfilled by the great cedar deity. Kaison, resembling a tengu, helped establish the tengu belief through his image, leading to the recognition of Hana-taka Tengu and Karasu Tengu as guardian deities. Hana-taka Tengu is known as the "Wish-fulfilling Tengu," and Karasu Tengu as the "Granting Tengu," believed to bestow blessings and fulfill wishes.
It worships a rarely worshipped [[kami]] named Anba sama.<ref name=":0" />
